passage:
Few categories in public international law have provoked as much enthusiasm, and as little analytical rigor, as the category of jus cogens — the small class of peremptory norms from which, it is said, no derogation is permitted. Since the International Law Commission's draft articles of 1966, commentators have treated jus cogens as the constitutional bedrock of the international legal order, a fixed point by reference to which lesser norms are to be tested. Yet a closer reading of the tribunals that have actually applied the concept suggests that this confidence is premature; the bedrock, if it exists, has been charted almost entirely from above.

Consider the 2011 advisory opinion of the Federation of Isuria's regional human-rights court, widely cited for the proposition that the prohibition of enforced disappearance has acquired peremptory status. The court purported to identify this status by surveying the practice of states, the pronouncements of treaty bodies, and the writings of publicists. On inspection, however, the state practice catalogued was thin, the treaty-body pronouncements largely circular (each citing the others), and the publicists predominantly the court's own former members. The court did not so much discover a peremptory norm as ratify one; and the ratification was, in the opinion's own words, "the culmination of a juridical conscience whose outlines the tribunal has already traced." Whether that culmination reflects opinio juris in the traditional sense — a belief among states that they are legally bound — or merely the opinio juris of the judges, is a question the opinion conspicuously declines to press.

A defender of the tribunal might reply that peremptory norms, precisely because they express values that transcend state consent, need not be established by the ordinary inductive methods of customary international law. This reply has the merit of candor, but it concedes the point. Once it is conceded that jus cogens is not a subset of customary norms distinguished by their gravity, but an independent category established by judicial declaration, the notion that such norms furnish an external check on state conduct becomes difficult to sustain. The check is internal to the juridical order that identifies it.

This is not to deny that certain prohibitions — of genocide, of slavery, of aggressive war — command a degree of assent that ordinary treaty norms do not. What is denied is that the current doctrine has given a stable account of how such prohibitions are to be identified, or of what work the peremptory label does beyond signaling the tribunal's own sense of moral urgency. Until that account is supplied, the category will continue to be invoked, regrettably, as a rhetorical resource rather than as a rule of recognition.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The doctrine of jus cogens lacks a principled method of identification and therefore functions less as an external constraint on state conduct than as a vehicle for judicial moral commitments.

choices.label: B
choices.text: International tribunals that have attempted to identify peremptory norms have consistently misapplied the inductive techniques of customary international law.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The prohibitions of genocide, slavery, and aggressive war, whatever their standing in positive law, are not properly characterized as peremptory norms.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Commentators since the International Law Commission's 1966 draft articles have correctly identified jus cogens as the constitutional bedrock of the international legal order.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The Federation of Isuria's regional human-rights court erred in its 2011 advisory opinion by relying on the writings of its own former members.

explanations.correct: The author sets up the enthusiasm for jus cogens, uses the Isuria opinion to expose the circularity of its identification, concedes that certain prohibitions command wide assent, and closes by insisting that until a stable account of identification is supplied the category operates as rhetoric rather than as a rule of recognition. A captures that integrated thesis.
explanations.B: Too narrow — the author's deeper claim is that peremptory norms may not be a subset of customary norms at all; the critique is not merely of inductive technique.
explanations.C: Reverses the author, who explicitly concedes these prohibitions command unusual assent and denies only that the current doctrine explains how such norms are identified.
explanations.D: Restates the view the author is criticizing.
explanations.E: Paragraph-level restatement fixating on one illustrative case rather than the broader doctrinal point.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward the defense of the tribunal offered at the beginning of the third paragraph can most accurately be described as

choices.label: A
choices.text: initial sympathy that gives way to outright rejection on the ground that the defense misreads the tribunal's own reasoning

choices.label: B
choices.text: qualified acknowledgment of its candor combined with the judgment that it concedes the very point at issue

choices.label: C
choices.text: unqualified endorsement, since the defense rightly insists that peremptory norms transcend state consent

choices.label: D
choices.text: polite dismissal, on the ground that the defense is inconsistent with the inductive methods of customary international law

choices.label: E
choices.text: puzzled agnosticism, since the defense rests on philosophical premises the author has not evaluated

explanations.correct: The author says the reply 'has the merit of candor, but it concedes the point.' That is the exact structure: acknowledgment of candor plus the judgment that the defense gives away what it was meant to save.
explanations.A: Overstates: the author does not reject the defense as a misreading; he accepts its candor and turns its concession against it.
explanations.C: The author does not endorse the defense; he uses it to derive an unwelcome conclusion.
explanations.D: The author does not accuse the defense of inconsistency with inductive method; that is the trouble with the tribunal's practice, not with the defense.
explanations.E: Out of register — the author reaches a definite judgment.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that the author would agree with which one of the following statements about the relationship between jus cogens and customary international law?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Jus cogens is best understood as a subset of customary norms distinguished from other such norms by the gravity of the interests they protect.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The inductive techniques used to identify customary norms are inadequate to the task of identifying peremptory norms and should be abandoned in favor of judicial declaration.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Were peremptory norms established by the same inductive survey of state practice and opinio juris used for customary norms, they could plausibly serve as an external check on state conduct.

choices.label: D
choices.text: There is no meaningful difference between the authority of ordinary customary norms and the authority of putatively peremptory norms.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The category of jus cogens is coherent in principle but has been badly applied by tribunals; with better-trained judges, the difficulties would dissolve.

explanations.correct: The author's critique is that once jus cogens is detached from inductive identification through state practice, it ceases to be external to the juridical order. The converse — the inference the author has not stated but would accept — is that inductive grounding would restore the external-check function. C articulates that converse precisely and in hedged terms.
explanations.A: The author's defender offers this formulation in order to reject it; the author declines to endorse it, since the tribunals have not in fact identified peremptory norms through the ordinary inductive methods.
explanations.B: Reverses the author: he criticizes judicial declaration and treats inductive methods as the alternative whose abandonment is the problem.
explanations.D: Too strong — the author concedes that certain prohibitions command unusual assent and does not deny a difference in degree.
explanations.E: The author's critique is structural, not a matter of better training; he says the doctrine has not supplied a stable account.

questions.questionStem: The author's discussion of the 2011 Isuria advisory opinion in the second paragraph functions primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: offer an illustrative case in which the standard inductive method for identifying customary norms was properly applied

choices.label: B
choices.text: demonstrate that the tribunal's methodology collapsed into self-reference, thereby supporting the author's broader claim that peremptory norms have been charted from within the juridical order rather than discovered outside it

choices.label: C
choices.text: concede that even a flawed identification of a peremptory norm is preferable to no identification at all

choices.label: D
choices.text: contrast the Isuria court's approach with the more rigorous approach of the International Law Commission's 1966 draft articles

choices.label: E
choices.text: argue that the prohibition of enforced disappearance has not in fact achieved the degree of assent that genocide and slavery command

explanations.correct: The second paragraph is doing work for the metaphor introduced at the end of paragraph 1: the 'bedrock charted from above.' The thin state practice, the circular treaty-body citations, and the court's own former members as publicists together show self-reference, which is what the thesis needs to be demonstrated.
explanations.A: Reverses the function: the example is offered as a failure of inductive method, not a success.
explanations.C: The author does not concede this; he denies the identification does the work claimed.
explanations.D: The ILC draft is mentioned only as the origin of the enthusiasm the author is criticizing; no rigor contrast is developed.
explanations.E: The author is silent on whether the specific prohibition has wide assent; his critique is about the method of identification, not the substantive standing of this norm.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, which one of the following features of the 2011 Isuria advisory opinion's reasoning did the author identify as problematic?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It relied on the writings of publicists who were not themselves former members of the tribunal.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It refused to consult the pronouncements of treaty bodies on the question of enforced disappearance.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It treated the opinio juris of judges as evidence of the opinio juris of states without pressing the distinction between the two.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It departed from the International Law Commission's 1966 draft articles in its definition of peremptory status.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It identified a peremptory norm without also surveying the practice of states.

explanations.correct: The author writes that 'whether that culmination reflects opinio juris in the traditional sense — a belief among states that they are legally bound — or merely the opinio juris of the judges, is a question the opinion conspicuously declines to press.' C paraphrases exactly that complaint.
explanations.A: Inverts the detail: the author complains that the publicists were predominantly the court's former members.
explanations.B: Wrong sentence: the author notes that treaty-body pronouncements were consulted but were largely circular.
explanations.D: The author does not contrast the opinion with the 1966 draft articles on the definition of peremptory status.
explanations.E: The author says state practice was catalogued but thin, not that no survey was conducted.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following situations most closely conforms to the structural problem the author identifies with the current doctrine of jus cogens?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A scientific academy declares a novel result to be an established fact by surveying journal articles, most of which were authored by members of the academy and which chiefly cite one another.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A national supreme court strikes down a statute as unconstitutional by applying a long-settled textual canon of interpretation to the statute's language.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A professional association adopts a new ethical rule after a public comment period in which a majority of practitioners endorsed the rule in writing.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A regulatory agency issues a guidance document interpreting a statute the agency itself administers, basing the interpretation on the statute's legislative history.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A historian concludes that a disputed battle occurred on a particular date by triangulating among three independent archival sources maintained by different polities.

explanations.correct: The load-bearing structure the author identifies is self-reference masquerading as external discovery: the bedrock 'charted almost entirely from above,' with the court's own former members as publicists and treaty bodies citing one another. A reproduces that exact structure — a body declaring a truth by surveying sources that derive from itself and cite one another.
explanations.B: A shares the surface feature of authoritative pronouncement but instantiates a different mechanism: application of an established canon to text, not self-referential identification of a novel norm.
explanations.C: The public-comment mechanism introduces an external constituency rather than instantiating self-reference.
explanations.D: Administrative interpretation grounded in legislative history is not self-reference in the relevant sense; the agency is interpreting an externally given text.
explanations.E: Triangulation among three independent polities is precisely the external, inductive method the author says jus cogens doctrine lacks.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most undermine the author's argument that the current doctrine of jus cogens fails to furnish an external check on state conduct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A comprehensive empirical study demonstrates that, in the decade following the Isuria opinion, states whose practice the tribunal had not surveyed nevertheless altered their conduct to conform with the tribunal's identification of the peremptory norm, citing the tribunal's reasoning in their own official pronouncements.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Several commentators have objected to the Isuria opinion on the ground that its list of publicists included members who had served on the tribunal in earlier decades.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Other regional human-rights courts have issued advisory opinions identifying peremptory norms using methodologies similar to that of the Isuria tribunal.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The prohibitions of genocide and aggressive war were recognized as peremptory norms before the International Law Commission's 1966 draft articles.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A minority of states have rejected the Isuria opinion outright and have denied that the prohibition of enforced disappearance has peremptory status.

explanations.correct: The author's argument is that jus cogens lacks an external check because its identification is internal to the juridical order. If states not surveyed by the tribunal nevertheless conform their conduct to the tribunal's identification and cite the tribunal's reasoning as authority, then the identification does in practice operate on state conduct externally — which is the very function the author denies it performs. That most directly undermines the author's claim.
explanations.B: Echoes the author's own observation about the publicists rather than contradicting his structural critique.
explanations.C: Extends the pattern the author criticizes to other tribunals; it reinforces rather than undermines his diagnosis.
explanations.D: Says nothing about the method of identification or the external-check function.
explanations.E: Consistent with the author's picture: if a minority of states reject the norm outright, the supposed peremptory character does not constrain them, which cuts with rather than against the author.

passage:
For nearly four decades, the administrative courts of the Republic of Caltrana have been governed by what practitioners call the Two-Step: when an agency's interpretation of a statute it administers is challenged, the court asks first whether the statute is ambiguous, and, if it is, defers to any reasonable agency reading. The doctrine was announced in a 1987 case concerning a rulemaking on flue-gas emissions and has since become a fixture of the country's public law. What has gone insufficiently noticed, however, is that the Two-Step has quietly accreted a third step — one the court has never acknowledged — that now does much of the actual work.

The accretion began, on the better reading of the cases, with a 2002 dispute over pharmaceutical labeling. The reviewing chamber purported to apply the Two-Step but prefaced its analysis with the observation that the agency's interpretation must be consistent with the statute's "animating purpose." Later opinions have elaborated this preface into a threshold inquiry: before asking whether the statute is ambiguous, the court now asks whether the agency's reading sits comfortably within what the chamber calls the statute's "ordered scheme." Only interpretations that pass this unstated step proceed to the conventional ambiguity analysis. In effect, the court has reserved to itself a prior power to pronounce on statutory coherence — a power that the original doctrine deliberately withheld from reviewing courts, precisely because coherence judgments are sensitive to the same policy considerations that the doctrine wished to leave to the agency.

Defenders of the new approach describe it as an obvious refinement: no one, they say, would wish courts to defer to readings that are in tension with the statute's evident design. The point is not without force. Yet the defense misstates what the original doctrine required. Under the 1987 formulation, a reading in tension with statutory design would ordinarily fail at step two as unreasonable; the court had no occasion to reach that question until ambiguity had been established. The effect of inserting a coherence inquiry at the threshold is not to catch interpretations the old doctrine would have missed but to permit the court to reject interpretations without undertaking the ambiguity analysis that, by its own logic, should precede any such rejection.

Whether this development represents a welcome correction or a doctrinal drift will depend, one supposes, on how much faith one has in the reviewing courts' ability to distinguish coherence from policy preference. The present author is not sanguine. The doctrine's chief virtue, when first announced, was its discipline; the accreted third step, by inviting courts to identify statutory design without the constraint of ambiguity analysis, has begun to dissolve that discipline while continuing to invoke its name.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Caltranan administrative courts have grafted an unacknowledged coherence inquiry onto the Two-Step, and the inquiry has undermined the discipline that the original doctrine was designed to supply.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Defenders of the Caltranan courts' recent approach are correct that no agency interpretation in tension with statutory design should receive deference.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The 1987 Two-Step doctrine has been overtaken by more recent decisions that explicitly repudiate its premises.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reviewing courts are institutionally incapable of distinguishing judgments of statutory coherence from judgments of policy preference.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The 2002 dispute over pharmaceutical labeling should be regarded as the moment when the Two-Step doctrine ceased to be good law in Caltrana.

explanations.correct: The passage identifies a quiet accretion of a third step, traces it to the 2002 pharmaceutical case, argues that its defenders misstate the original doctrine, and closes by judging that the accretion has begun to dissolve the discipline the original doctrine was designed to supply. A captures both the descriptive and evaluative strands.
explanations.B: Restates the defenders' view, which the author treats as partly forceful but ultimately mistaken.
explanations.C: Too strong — the courts continue to invoke the Two-Step; the author's complaint is precisely that they do so while modifying it in substance.
explanations.D: A proposition the author's concluding skepticism is consistent with but does not establish as the main claim; the main claim is doctrinal, not epistemic-general.
explanations.E: Paragraph-level restatement fixating on the 2002 case.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An established doctrine is described; an unacknowledged modification is identified and traced to a specific case; a defense of the modification is presented and rebutted; the author offers a skeptical concluding assessment.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Two rival interpretations of a statute are presented; the arguments for each are surveyed; the author concludes that the second is more faithful to the statute's design.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A doctrine is described; its historical origins are traced; an analogous doctrine in a foreign jurisdiction is introduced as a superior model; the two are compared.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A judicial decision is summarized; its reasoning is criticized as internally inconsistent; a proposed correction is offered; the correction is shown to resolve the doctrinal difficulty.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A practice is defended against a familiar objection; the objection is shown to rest on a misunderstanding; the defense is extended to a range of adjacent practices.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 describes the Two-Step and flags the accreted third step; paragraph 2 traces the accretion to the 2002 pharmaceutical case and elaborates the unstated coherence inquiry; paragraph 3 presents the defenders' view and rebuts it; paragraph 4 offers the author's skeptical concluding assessment. A maps this sequence correctly.
explanations.B: The passage is about a doctrine's evolution, not a choice between two statutory interpretations.
explanations.D: The author does not propose a correction that resolves the difficulty; he diagnoses a drift.
explanations.E: Reverses the posture: a defense is presented and rebutted, not extended.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that the author would accept which one of the following claims about the 1987 Two-Step as originally formulated?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It permitted reviewing courts to reject an agency interpretation on the ground of statutory incoherence only after a finding that the statute was ambiguous.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It required agencies to adopt interpretations consistent with a statute's animating purpose as determined by the reviewing court in advance of any deference.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It made no provision for reviewing courts to reject unreasonable agency interpretations at any stage of the analysis.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It was formulated with an implicit understanding that future courts would supplement it with a threshold coherence inquiry.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It applied only to rulemakings concerning environmental emissions and did not govern agency interpretations in other areas.

explanations.correct: The author says that under the 1987 formulation, a reading in tension with statutory design would ordinarily fail at step two as unreasonable, and that the court had no occasion to reach that question until ambiguity had been established. A restates that commitment: rejection on coherence grounds occurred only after a finding of ambiguity.
explanations.B: Describes the accreted third step, which the author treats as a departure from, not a feature of, the 1987 doctrine.
explanations.C: Reverses the author, who explicitly says unreasonable interpretations could be rejected at step two.
explanations.D: The author characterizes the third step as unacknowledged and as 'doctrinal drift,' not as an anticipated supplement.
explanations.E: Outside scope — the author calls the doctrine 'a fixture of the country's public law,' not confined to emissions.

questions.questionStem: The author's observation in the third paragraph that the defenders' point is "not without force" functions primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: concede the plausibility of the defense before arguing that it rests on a mischaracterization of what the original doctrine required

choices.label: B
choices.text: introduce a counterexample that the author will ultimately treat as decisive against the original doctrine

choices.label: C
choices.text: signal the author's agreement with the defenders and preface the rejection of his earlier critique of the accreted third step

choices.label: D
choices.text: suggest that the coherence inquiry, although unacknowledged, has been applied in a manner consistent with the 1987 formulation

choices.label: E
choices.text: indicate that the author considers the defenders' position more persuasive than his own and is preparing to abandon his earlier diagnosis

explanations.correct: The phrase is the hinge of a classic concede-then-rebut move. The author grants that no one would wish courts to defer to readings in tension with statutory design, then uses the next two sentences to argue that the original doctrine already handled such readings at step two, so the refinement is not what the defenders claim it is.
explanations.B: The author does not treat the defenders' point as decisive against the original doctrine; he treats it as a concession he will absorb and then turn.
explanations.C: Reverses the passage: the author does not reject his earlier critique; he reinforces it.
explanations.D: The author's rebuttal denies that the third step is consistent with the original formulation.
explanations.E: Out of register — the author's closing 'not sanguine' shows he does not abandon his diagnosis.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward the reviewing courts' ability to distinguish judgments of statutory coherence from judgments of policy preference can most accurately be described as

choices.label: A
choices.text: confident that the courts possess the requisite capacity and exercise it reliably

choices.label: B
choices.text: guardedly doubtful, implying that the courts are not well positioned to maintain the distinction in the absence of the constraint that ambiguity analysis formerly provided

choices.label: C
choices.text: entirely agnostic, regarding the question as unanswerable on the evidence the passage supplies

choices.label: D
choices.text: dismissive, denying that the distinction itself is coherent

choices.label: E
choices.text: openly contemptuous of the courts' institutional competence in administrative matters generally

explanations.correct: The author writes 'the present author is not sanguine,' and explains that the accreted third step has begun to 'dissolve' the doctrine's discipline by inviting courts to identify statutory design 'without the constraint of ambiguity analysis.' That is guarded doubt tied to a specific structural cause — exactly B.
explanations.C: The author reaches a judgment; he is not agnostic.
explanations.D: He does not deny that the distinction is coherent; he doubts that the courts will maintain it in practice.
explanations.E: Out of register — 'not sanguine' is measured, not contemptuous; the author addresses a specific doctrinal context, not the courts' general competence.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following judicial practices, if adopted in another area of law, would most closely conform to the structural development the author identifies in the Caltranan administrative courts?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A court reviewing a contract dispute begins to ask, before the conventional inquiry into whether the contract language is ambiguous, whether the proposed construction is consistent with the contract's general commercial design, and rejects constructions that fail that threshold without reaching the ambiguity inquiry.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A court reviewing a criminal sentence applies a deferential standard to the trial court's findings of fact but reviews legal conclusions de novo.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A court hearing a constitutional challenge subjects the challenged statute to a higher standard of review when it implicates a fundamental right than when it does not.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A court presiding over a jury trial instructs the jury to disregard evidence that the court has ruled inadmissible under established rules.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A court in a tort action declines to reach the question of damages until it has determined that the defendant is liable.

explanations.correct: The load-bearing structure is the insertion of an unacknowledged threshold inquiry into 'design' or 'scheme' before the conventional ambiguity analysis, which permits the court to reject interpretations without reaching the analysis that by its own logic should precede such rejection. A reproduces that exact structure in the contract-law setting.
explanations.B: Different standards for different issues is orthogonal to the threshold-inquiry mechanism the author is describing.
explanations.C: Tiered scrutiny of statutes is not a hidden threshold; it is an openly applied doctrine selecting the level of review.
explanations.D: Evidentiary rulings are not threshold interpretive inquiries of the kind at issue.
explanations.E: Surface similarity — issue-ordering — but the liability-before-damages order is the conventional sequence that has always been required, not an accreted threshold that displaces an earlier analytic step.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that the author would regard which one of the following hypothetical judicial practices as consistent with the original 1987 doctrine?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A chamber finds that the statute at issue is ambiguous, considers the agency's reading, and rejects that reading as unreasonable because it cannot be squared with the statute's design.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A chamber rejects the agency's reading at the threshold on the ground that the reading does not sit comfortably within the statute's ordered scheme.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A chamber defers to the agency's reading without considering whether the statute is ambiguous, on the ground that agencies generally possess greater expertise than courts.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A chamber refuses to apply the Two-Step to interpretations of statutes that were enacted before the 1987 decision.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A chamber treats its own prior characterizations of a statute's animating purpose as binding in all future cases interpreting that statute.

explanations.correct: The author writes that under the 1987 formulation, a reading in tension with statutory design would ordinarily fail at step two as unreasonable — precisely what the chamber in A does, by first finding ambiguity and then rejecting the agency's reading as unreasonable on design grounds.
explanations.B: Describes the accreted third step the author is criticizing, not the original doctrine.
explanations.C: Skips the ambiguity analysis altogether and so is not the original doctrine either.
explanations.D: The passage gives no indication that the 1987 doctrine was limited to post-1987 statutes.
explanations.E: The passage says nothing to support binding-precedent status for a chamber's purpose-characterizations across future cases.
